items.answer: The MANN-WHITNEY U TEST (also called WILCOXON RANK-SUM TEST) is a nonparametric test for comparing the distributions of two independent samples. It tests whether one distribution tends to have larger values than the other (a shift in location, more generally stochastic dominance). Setup: X_1,...,X_{n_1} from distribution F, Y_1,...,Y_{n_2} from distribution G, independent. H_0: F = G (equal distributions) vs H_1: F != G (or one-sided: X tends smaller/larger than Y). PROCEDURE (rank-sum form): (1) POOL all n_1 + n_2 observations; (2) rank them from 1 (smallest) to n_1+n_2 (largest), using average ranks for ties; (3) compute R_X = sum of ranks of the X observations; (4) the test statistic is W = R_X (Wilcoxon form) or equivalently U = R_X - n_1(n_1+1)/2 (Mann-Whitney form). U counts the number of (X_i, Y_j) pairs with X_i > Y_j (plus 1/2 for ties). RELATIONSHIP: U = #{(i,j): X_i > Y_j} + (1/2) #{(i,j): X_i = Y_j}. Under H_0, E[U] = n_1 n_2 / 2, Var(U) = n_1 n_2 (n_1+n_2+1)/12 (with tie correction). EXACT null distribution: available from tables for small samples. NORMAL APPROXIMATION (n_1, n_2 >= 10): Z = (U - n_1 n_2/2) / sqrt(n_1 n_2 (n_1+n_2+1)/12) ~ N(0,1). Reject for large |Z|. EXAMPLE: n_1=5, n_2=6. X ranks (out of 11): [2, 4, 6, 8, 10], R_X = 30. U = 30 - 5*6/2 = 30 - 15 = 15. E[U] = 5*6/2 = 15, Var = 5*6*12/12 = 30, SD = 5.48. Z = 0. Two-sided p = 1.0 (no evidence of difference). INTERPRETATION: rejecting H_0 means the distributions differ in location (one tends to have larger values). ADVANTAGES: (1) nonparametric (no normality, no equal-variance assumption); (2) tests a more general hypothesis than the t-test (stochastic dominance vs just mean equality); (3) ARE vs t-test for normal data = 3/pi approx 0.955 (nearly as efficient; MORE efficient for heavy-tailed distributions like logistic or double-exponential). EQUIVALENCE: the Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon rank-sum are algebraically equivalent (U = W - n_1(n_1+1)/2). The Mann-Whitney U test is the standard nonparametric alternative to the two-sample t-test.

items.question: What is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test?
items.answer: The KOLMOGOROV-SMIRNOV (KS) TEST is a nonparametric test comparing a sample distribution to a reference distribution (one-sample) or comparing two sample distributions (two-sample). It is based on the MAXIMUM vertical distance between empirical and theoretical CDFs. ONE-SAMPLE KS: test H_0: sample comes from distribution F_0. Test statistic D = sup_x |F_n(x) - F_0(x)|, where F_n is the empirical CDF. Under H_0, sqrt(n) D ->^D K (the Kolmogorov distribution), with P(sqrt(n) D <= x) -> 1 - 2 sum_{k=1}^inf (-1)^{k-1} exp(-2 k^2 x^2). Critical values: D_{n, alpha} approx c_alpha / sqrt(n), where c_{0.05} = 1.358, c_{0.01} = 1.628. Reject if D > D_{n, alpha}. TWO-SAMPLE KS: test H_0: F_X = F_Y for two independent samples. Test statistic D = sup_x |F_{n_1}(x) - G_{n_2}(x)|. Under H_0, sqrt(n_1 n_2/(n_1+n_2)) D ->^D K. EXAMPLE (one-sample): test if 20 observations are N(0,1). Compute F_n at each data point, compare to Phi, find max difference D = 0.31. Critical D_{20, 0.05} = 1.358/sqrt(20) = 0.304. 0.31 > 0.304, reject H_0. ADVANTAGES: (1) nonparametric, distribution-free (under H_0 the null distribution of D does not depend on F_0 if F_0 is continuous); (2) tests the ENTIRE distribution (not just location or variance); (3) no binning required (unlike chi-squared GOF). DISADVANTAGES: (1) more sensitive near the CENTER of the distribution than the tails (since F_n changes fastest there); (2) the null distribution changes if parameters are estimated (Lilliefors correction for testing normality with estimated mu, sigma); (3) generally LOWER POWER than specialized tests (Anderson-Darling for distributional fit, Shapiro-Wilk for normality). VARIANTS: (1) ANDERSON-DARLING — weighted integral of (F_n - F_0)^2 / [F_0(1-F_0)], more sensitive to tails; (2) CRAMER-VON MISES — unweighted integral of (F_n - F_0)^2; (3) KUIPER'S TEST — variant for circular data, D+ + D-. The KS test is widely used for distributional goodness-of-fit and two-sample comparison, especially in physics and finance.

items.question: What is a permutation test (randomization test)?
items.answer: A PERMUTATION TEST (also called RANDOMIZATION TEST) is a nonparametric test that computes the null distribution of a test statistic by RANDOMLY REPERMUTING the labels of the observations. It is EXACT (no asymptotic approximation) under the assumption of EXCHANGEABILITY under H_0. SETUP (two-sample): X_1,...,X_{n_1} (group A) and Y_1,...,Y_{n_2} (group B), test H_0: the two groups have the same distribution vs H_1: they differ. Procedure: (1) choose a test statistic T (e.g., |Xbar - Ybar|, or difference in medians, or any statistic); (2) POOL all n = n_1 + n_2 observations; (3) under H_0 (exchangeability), all C(n, n_1) ways of choosing n_1 observations to be "group A" are equally likely; (4) compute T for all (or many random) permutations; (5) the p-value = (number of permutations with T_perm >= T_observed) / (total number of permutations). EXACT PERMUTATION TEST: enumerate all C(n, n_1) permutations (feasible only for small n; e.g., C(20,10) = 184,756). MONTE CARLO PERMUTATION TEST: for large n, randomly sample B permutations (e.g., B=10000) and compute p = (1 + #{T_perm >= T_obs}) / (B + 1). EXAMPLE: n_1=n_2=5, test difference in means. Observed Xbar - Ybar = 2.3. All C(10,5) = 252 permutations computed; 6 permutations give |diff| >= 2.3. p = 6/252 = 0.024. Reject at alpha=0.05. PROPERTIES: (1) EXACT level alpha under H_0 (no large-sample approximation); (2) the test is VALID for any test statistic (mean, median, trimmed mean, t-statistic) — the permutation distribution is exact; (3) POWER depends on the choice of statistic — using the t-statistic gives a test asymptotically equivalent to the t-test; (4) the test is DISTRIBUTION-FREE under exchangeability. ADVANTAGES: (1) no parametric assumptions (normality, equal variance); (2) exact p-values; (3) flexible choice of test statistic; (4) naturally handles complex data structures (e.g., stratified, clustered — use restricted permutations). DISADVANTAGES: (1) computationally expensive for large n (Monte Carlo helps); (2) tests a slightly different null (exchangeability) than the t-test (equality of means); (3) can have lower power than parametric tests when parametric assumptions hold. APPLICATIONS: (1) A/B testing with non-normal data; (2) genomic data analysis (gene set enrichment); (3) causal inference (Fisher's exact test for randomization in experiments). The permutation test is the gold standard for nonparametric hypothesis testing and underlies the randomization inference framework.

items.question: What is bootstrap hypothesis testing?
items.answer: BOOTSTRAP HYPOTHESIS TESTING uses the bootstrap (resampling with replacement) to approximate the null distribution of a test statistic, especially when no parametric null distribution is available. Unlike the permutation test (which requires exchangeability under H_0), the bootstrap can handle settings where the null imposes a specific constraint (e.g., a specific parameter value) that is not naturally a permutation. SETUP: test H_0: theta = theta_0 vs H_1: theta != theta_0 using statistic T = T(X_1,...,X_n) (e.g., T = theta_hat - theta_0). Procedure (PARAMETRIC bootstrap): (1) estimate theta under H_0 (theta = theta_0); (2) generate B bootstrap samples from the model with theta = theta_0; (3) for each, compute T*_b = T(bootstrap sample) - theta_0; (4) the bootstrap null distribution of T is approximated by {T*_1,...,T*_B}; (5) p-value = (#{|T*_b| >= |T_obs|}) / B. Procedure (NONPARAMETRIC bootstrap): (1) resample with replacement from the OBSERVED data, but TRANSFORM to enforce H_0 (e.g., resample X_i and shift by theta_hat - theta_0 so that the resampled data has mean theta_0); (2) compute T*_b; (3) same p-value. EXAMPLE: test H_0: median = 5 using a sample of n=50. Observed median = 5.7. Nonparametric bootstrap: shift data so median = 5 (subtract 0.7), resample B=10000 times, compute median of each. Suppose 200 bootstrap medians have |median - 5| >= 0.7. p = 200/10000 = 0.02. Reject at alpha=0.05. ADVANTAGES: (1) works for any test statistic (median, trimmed mean, quantile, complex functional); (2) does not require normality or large-sample theory; (3) can handle nuisance parameters (resample under H_0 estimate). DISADVANTAGES: (1) computationally expensive (B = 1000-10000 resamples); (2) the bootstrap null distribution is only asymptotically correct (small-sample accuracy depends on the method); (3) requires careful construction to enforce H_0 (just resampling the data does not test H_0 — must resample under H_0). VARIANTS: (1) BOOTSTRAP T (studentized bootstrap) — resample a studentized statistic T/SE, more accurate; (2) BCA bootstrap (bias-corrected and accelerated) — for confidence intervals; (3) PERMUTATION vs BOOTSTRAP: permutation is exact for exchangeability nulls; bootstrap is more flexible but only asymptotic. APPLICATIONS: testing on complex statistics (medians, ratios, correlations), small-sample inference where parametric tests are unreliable, causal inference (bootstrap standard errors for treatment effect estimates). Bootstrap testing is a general-purpose computational method for nonparametric inference.

items.question: Worked example: find the Neyman-Pearson most powerful test for a simple normal mean.
items.answer: PROBLEM: X_1,...,X_n iid N(mu, 1) (known variance sigma^2=1). Test H_0: mu = 0 vs H_1: mu = 1 (simple vs simple) at level alpha = 0.05. Find the most powerful test. SOLUTION: By the Neyman-Pearson lemma, the MP test rejects H_0 when the likelihood ratio LR = L(mu=1)/L(mu=0) > k. Compute LR: L(mu) = (2pi)^{-n/2} exp[-(1/2) sum(X_i - mu)^2]. So LR = exp[-(1/2) sum(X_i - 1)^2 + (1/2) sum(X_i - 0)^2] = exp[-(1/2)(sum X_i^2 - 2 sum X_i + n) + (1/2) sum X_i^2] = exp[sum X_i - n/2] = exp[n Xbar - n/2]. LR is an increasing function of Xbar (since the exponent n Xbar - n/2 increases with Xbar). So reject H_0 when Xbar > c, where c is chosen so P_{mu=0}(Xbar > c) = 0.05. Under H_0, Xbar ~ N(0, 1/n), so sqrt(n) Xbar ~ N(0,1). P(Xbar > c) = P(Z > sqrt(n) c) = 0.05 -> sqrt(n) c = z_{0.95} = 1.645 -> c = 1.645/sqrt(n). So the MP test rejects when Xbar > 1.645/sqrt(n), equivalently when sum X_i > 1.645 sqrt(n). For n = 10: reject when Xbar > 1.645/sqrt(10) = 0.520, i.e., sum X_i > 5.20. POWER at mu = 1: power = P_{mu=1}(Xbar > 0.520) = P(N(1, 1/10) > 0.520) = P(Z > (0.520 - 1)/sqrt(0.1)) = P(Z > -0.480/0.316) = P(Z > -1.518) = Phi(1.518) = 0.936. So the MP test at level 0.05 has power 93.6% to detect mu=1 with n=10. CHECK: this is also the UMP test for H_0: mu <= 0 vs H_1: mu > 0 (by Karlin-Rubin, since the normal family has MLR in Xbar). The key steps: (1) write down the likelihood ratio; (2) simplify to identify the monotone function of the sufficient statistic; (3) determine the threshold from the null distribution; (4) compute power from the alternative distribution.

items.question: Worked example: find the UMP test for the exponential rate parameter.
items.answer: PROBLEM: X_1,...,X_n iid Exp(lambda) (density f(x|lambda) = lambda exp(-lambda x), x > 0). Test H_0: lambda >= lambda_0 vs H_1: lambda < lambda_0 (lower-tail) at level alpha. Find the UMP test. SOLUTION: The exponential family has density f(x|lambda) = lambda exp(-lambda x) = h(x) exp{-lambda x + log lambda}. This is a one-parameter exponential family with natural parameter eta = -lambda (decreasing in lambda) and sufficient statistic T = sum X_i. MLR: for lambda_1 < lambda_0 (alternative), f(x|lambda_1)/f(x|lambda_0) = (lambda_1/lambda_0)^n exp((lambda_0 - lambda_1) sum X_i), which is INCREASING in sum X_i (since lambda_0 - lambda_1 > 0). So the family has MLR in T = sum X_i (increasing). By Karlin-Rubin, for H_0: lambda >= lambda_0 vs H_1: lambda < lambda_0, we want to reject for LARGE values of the MLR statistic, but since smaller lambda means larger sum X_i (expensive tails), the rejection is for LARGE sum X_i. Wait — let me re-examine. For H_0: lambda >= lambda_0 vs H_1: lambda < lambda_0: lambda is smaller in the alternative, meaning the mean 1/lambda is LARGER, so we expect sum X_i to be larger under H_1. Reject for sum X_i > c. NULL DISTRIBUTION: under lambda_0, sum X_i ~ Gamma(n, lambda_0) (shape n, rate lambda_0). Equivalently 2 lambda_0 sum X_i ~ chi-squared_{2n}. Choose c so P_{lambda_0}(sum X_i > c) = alpha: c = (1/(2 lambda_0)) chi-squared_{2n, 1-alpha}. TEST: reject H_0 when sum X_i > chi-squared_{2n, 1-alpha} / (2 lambda_0). NUMERICAL EXAMPLE: n=10, lambda_0=2, alpha=0.05. chi-squared_{20, 0.95} = 31.41. c = 31.41 / (2*2) = 7.85. Reject if sum X_i > 7.85. Under H_0 (lambda=2), E[sum X_i] = n/lambda_0 = 10/2 = 5, so the threshold 7.85 is in the right tail. POWER at lambda_1 = 1 (smaller rate, larger mean): power = P_{lambda=1}(sum X_i > 7.85) = P(Gamma(10,1) > 7.85) = P(chi-squared_{20} > 2*1*7.85) = P(chi-squared_{20} > 15.7) = 1 - F_{chi^2_{20}}(15.7) approx 0.73. This is a UMP test (by Karlin-Rubin) because the exponential family has MLR in sum X_i.

items.question: Worked example: likelihood ratio test for normal variance — find the critical region.
items.answer: PROBLEM: X_1,...,X_n iid N(0, sigma^2) (mean KNOWN = 0). Test H_0: sigma^2 = 1 vs H_1: sigma^2 != 1 at level alpha. Derive the LRT and identify the critical region. SOLUTION: The log-likelihood: logL(sigma^2) = -(n/2) log(2 pi sigma^2) - (1/(2 sigma^2)) sum X_i^2. UNRESTRICTED MLE: d logL / d sigma^2 = -n/(2 sigma^2) + sum X_i^2 / (2 sigma^4) = 0 -> sigma_hat^2 = (1/n) sum X_i^2 = T/n, where T = sum X_i^2. RESTRICTED MLE (under H_0: sigma^2=1): sigma_hat_0^2 = 1 (no optimization needed — it is fixed at the null value). LRT STATISTIC: Lambda = L(sigma_hat_0^2) / L(sigma_hat^2) = L(1) / L(T/n). Compute: L(1) = (2pi)^{-n/2} exp(-T/2). L(T/n) = (2pi T/n)^{-n/2} exp(-n/2). So Lambda = (2pi)^{-n/2} exp(-T/2) / [(2pi T/n)^{-n/2} exp(-n/2)] = (T/n)^{n/2} exp(-T/2 + n/2) = (T/n)^{n/2} exp((n-T)/2). REJECT for SMALL Lambda. Analyze Lambda as a function of T: log Lambda = (n/2) log(T/n) + (n-T)/2 = (n/2)(log T - log n) + (n-T)/2. Take derivative: d log Lambda / dT = (n/2)(1/T) - 1/2 = (n/T - 1)/2 = (n - T)/(2T). So Lambda is maximized at T = n (where d log Lambda / dT = 0) and decreases as T moves away from n in EITHER direction (Lambda -> 0 as T -> 0 or T -> infinity). CRITICAL REGION: reject when T < c_1 OR T > c_2, where T = sum X_i^2. Under H_0 (sigma^2=1), T = sum X_i^2 ~ chi-squared_n. Choose c_1, c_2 so P(chi-squared_n < c_1) = alpha/2 and P(chi-squared_n > c_2) = alpha/2: c_1 = chi-squared_{n, alpha/2}, c_2 = chi-squared_{n, 1-alpha/2}. This is the equal-tail chi-squared test. NUMERICAL EXAMPLE: n=20, alpha=0.05. chi-squared_{20, 0.025} = 9.59, chi-squared_{20, 0.975} = 34.17. Reject H_0: sigma^2 = 1 if sum X_i^2 < 9.59 or sum X_i^2 > 34.17.

items.question: Worked example: two-sample pooled t-test with numbers.
Worked example: chi-squared goodness-of-fit test for die fairness.
items.answer: PROBLEM: A die is rolled 120 times. Observed counts: [25, 17, 15, 23, 19, 21] for faces 1-6. Test H_0: the die is fair (p_i = 1/6) at alpha = 0.05. SOLUTION: Step 1 — expected counts under H_0: E_i = n * p_i = 120 * (1/6) = 20 for each face. Step 2 — chi-squared statistic: X^2 = sum (O_i - E_i)^2 / E_i = (25-20)^2/20 + (17-20)^2/20 + (15-20)^2/20 + (23-20)^2/20 + (19-20)^2/20 + (21-20)^2/20 = (25 + 9 + 25 + 9 + 1 + 1)/20 = 70/20 = 3.5. Step 3 — degrees of freedom: k - 1 - m = 6 - 1 - 0 = 5 (no parameters estimated). Step 4 — critical value: chi-squared_{5, 0.95} = 11.07. Step 5 — decision: 3.5 < 11.07, FAIL TO REJECT H_0. The die appears fair. p-value: P(chi-squared_5 > 3.5) approx 0.62 (no evidence against fairness). Step 6 — check assumptions: all E_i = 20 >= 5, so the chi-squared approximation is valid. INTERPRETATION: although the observed counts deviate from 20 (e.g., face 1 appears 25 times, face 3 only 15 times), these deviations are within the range expected by chance for 120 rolls of a fair die. If we had observed [30, 12, 14, 22, 18, 24] instead, X^2 = (100 + 64 + 36 + 4 + 4 + 16)/20 = 224/20 = 11.2 > 11.07, which WOULD reject H_0. EXTENSION — if H_0 was "die follows probabilities p = [0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.2, 0.15, 0.2]" (not uniform), the expected counts would be E_i = 120 p_i, same X^2 formula, df = 5 (no estimated parameters). If we estimated a parameter (e.g., tested fit to Poisson with estimated lambda), df = k - 1 - m where m is the number of estimated parameters.

items.question: Worked example: Wilcoxon signed-rank test small sample.
items.answer: PROBLEM: 8 patients measure blood pressure before and after a drug. Differences (after - before): [-3, +5, +2, -1, +6, +4, -2, +3]. Test H_0: median difference = 0 vs H_1: median difference != 0 at alpha = 0.05 (two-sided). SOLUTION: Step 1 — compute |D_i|: [3, 5, 2, 1, 6, 4, 2, 3]. Step 2 — rank the |D_i| from smallest to largest. Sorted: [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Assign ranks (with ties averaged): rank 1 -> value 1; ranks 2 and 3 (avg 2.5) -> the two values of 2; ranks 4 and 5 (avg 4.5) -> the two values of 3; rank 6 -> value 4; rank 7 -> value 5; rank 8 -> value 6. So ranks: D=-3 (|D|=3, rank 4.5), D=+5 (rank 7), D=+2 (|D|=2, rank 2.5), D=-1 (rank 1), D=+6 (rank 8), D=+4 (rank 6), D=-2 (|D|=2, rank 2.5), D=+3 (|D|=3, rank 4.5). Step 3 — compute W+ = sum of ranks where D > 0: D=+5 (rank 7), D=+2 (rank 2.5), D=+6 (rank 8), D=+4 (rank 6), D=+3 (rank 4.5). W+ = 7 + 2.5 + 8 + 6 + 4.5 = 28. Step 4 — null distribution: under H_0, E[W+] = n(n+1)/4 = 8*9/4 = 18, Var(W+) = n(n+1)(2n+1)/24 = 8*9*17/24 = 51 (with tie adjustment slightly less). SD = sqrt(51) = 7.14. Step 5 — normal approximation: Z = (W+ - 18)/7.14 = (28 - 18)/7.14 = 10/7.14 = 1.40. Step 6 — decision (two-sided, alpha=0.05): critical z = 1.96. |Z| = 1.40 < 1.96, FAIL TO REJECT H_0. p-value = 2(1 - Phi(1.40)) = 2 * 0.0808 = 0.162. INTERPRETATION: although 5 of 8 differences are positive (and W+ = 28 > E[W+] = 18), the evidence is not strong enough at alpha=0.05 to conclude a systematic shift. With only n=8, the test has low power. EXACT p-value (from tables): for n=8, two-sided exact p for W+ = 28 is approximately 0.16, consistent with the normal approximation. If we had observed more extreme W+ (e.g., W+ = 33), the exact p would be approximately 0.04, rejecting H_0. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is more powerful than the sign test here because it uses magnitudes (the large positive differences +5, +6 contribute more to W+ than the small negative differences -1, -2).

items.question: Worked example: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control on a list of p-values.
items.answer: PROBLEM: A genomic study tests 10 hypotheses (genes), producing p-values: [0.001, 0.008, 0.039, 0.041, 0.042, 0.060, 0.074, 0.205, 0.212, 0.216]. Apply the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure to control the False Discovery Rate at q = 0.05. Which hypotheses are rejected? SOLUTION: The BH procedure controls FDR (expected proportion of false positives among rejections). Step 1 — sort p-values in ascending order: already sorted p_{(1)}=0.001, p_{(2)}=0.008, p_{(3)}=0.039, p_{(4)}=0.041, p_{(5)}=0.042, p_{(6)}=0.060, p_{(7)}=0.074, p_{(8)}=0.205, p_{(9)}=0.212, p_{(10)}=0.216. Step 2 — compute BH thresholds: for rank k (k=1,...,m), threshold = k * q / m = k * 0.05 / 10 = 0.005 k. Thresholds: k=1: 0.005, k=2: 0.010, k=3: 0.015, k=4: 0.020, k=5: 0.025, k=6: 0.030, k=7: 0.035, k=8: 0.040, k=9: 0.045, k=10: 0.050. Step 3 — find the LARGEST k such that p_{(k)} <= k * q / m. Compare: k=1: 0.001 <= 0.005 (yes). k=2: 0.008 <= 0.010 (yes). k=3: 0.039 <= 0.015 (no). k=4: 0.041 <= 0.020 (no). k=5: 0.042 <= 0.025 (no). k=6: 0.060 <= 0.030 (no). k=7: 0.074 <= 0.035 (no). k=8: 0.205 <= 0.040 (no). k=9: 0.212 <= 0.045 (no). k=10: 0.216 <= 0.050 (no). The largest k satisfying the condition is k = 2. Step 4 — reject all hypotheses with rank <= k_max, i.e., reject H_{(1)} and H_{(2)} (p-values 0.001 and 0.008). Step 5 — report: 2 out of 10 hypotheses rejected, with FDR controlled at 5%. INTERPRETATION: even though several p-values are < 0.05 (0.039, 0.041, 0.042), the BH procedure does NOT reject them, because they fail the rank-adjusted threshold (they would be the 3rd, 4th, 5th smallest, and the corresponding thresholds 0.015, 0.020, 0.025 are stricter). The BH procedure is LESS CONSERVATIVE than Bonferroni (which would reject only p <= 0.05/10 = 0.005, i.e., only p=0.001) but MORE CONSERVATIVE than unadjusted (which would reject all p <= 0.05, i.e., 5 hypotheses). BH ADJUSTED p-VALUES (BH q-values): p_{(k)}^{adj} = min_{j>=k} [m p_{(j)} / j]. For k=10: 10*0.216/10 = 0.216. k=9: min(0.216, 10*0.212/9) = min(0.216, 0.236) = 0.216. ... k=2: min(..., 10*0.008/2) = 0.04. k=1: min(0.04, 10*0.001/1) = 0.01. So adjusted p-values: [0.01, 0.04, 0.13, 0.13, 0.13, 0.10, ...]. Rejecting at adjusted p <= 0.05 gives the same 2 hypotheses.
